rows: Suspected tuberculosis requires appropriate clinical investigation and notification.
Pulmonary and other infectious forms require timely public-health assessment.
Diagnosis uses clinical, radiological and microbiological evidence.
Contact tracing should reflect infectiousness, setting and exposure duration.
Treatment requires an appropriate multi-drug regimen and adherence support.
Drug-resistance testing informs treatment and public-health action.
Screening programmes target defined higher-risk groups.
Cases and outcomes contribute to national surveillance.
A cough, chest image or positive screening test does not alone establish active infectious tuberculosis.
Conclusions require symptoms, site, microbiology, imaging, infectious period, treatment, contacts and public-health evidence.
Invasive meningococcal disease is a medical emergency.
Suspected cases require urgent clinical treatment and public-health notification.
Laboratory samples support confirmation and typing.
Close contacts should be identified using defined exposure criteria.
Chemoprophylaxis is offered to specified close contacts.
Vaccination may be recommended according to strain and circumstances.
Healthcare exposure assessment depends on direct contact with respiratory secretions.
Clusters require coordinated epidemiological and microbiological investigation.
Fever, rash or shared accommodation does not establish meningococcal disease or close-contact status.
Conclusions require clinical syndrome, laboratory, timing, exposure, strain, prophylaxis and public-health evidence.
Streptococcus pneumoniae can cause invasive and non-invasive disease.
Invasive pneumococcal disease is monitored through laboratory surveillance.
Vaccination is used to protect defined age and clinical-risk groups.
Specimen and isolate information support diagnosis and surveillance.
Serotype data help assess vaccine impact and emerging patterns.
Clinical management depends on disease site, severity and antimicrobial susceptibility.
Clusters or unusual events may require public-health assessment.
Current immunisation guidance should be used for vaccine decisions.
A positive respiratory sample or vaccination record does not establish invasive disease or immunity.
Conclusions require specimen site, clinical syndrome, culture or molecular result, serotype, vaccination and epidemiological evidence.
Chickenpox is caused by varicella-zoster virus and is highly transmissible.
Case assessment should consider rash onset, clinical features and exposure.
People at increased risk of severe disease require prompt specialist assessment after exposure.
Pregnant people and immunocompromised contacts need risk-based management.
Post-exposure prophylaxis may include antiviral treatment or immunoglobulin according to current guidance.
Healthcare and institutional settings require setting-specific infection-control action.
Cases should avoid contact with susceptible high-risk people while infectious.
Outbreak management should use current UKHSA guidance.
A vesicular rash or reported contact does not establish chickenpox or susceptibility.
Conclusions require clinical features, timing, immunity, pregnancy or immune status, exposure and specialist evidence.
